intro: This is lsm-tree, a crash-safe storage engine I built from scratch in C++. Everything in this video runs for real, on the real code, with no mocks.
tests: First, the test suite. More than eight thousand assertions cover recovery, leveled compaction, snapshots, and writers racing readers.
asan: Next, the same suite under AddressSanitizer and undefined-behavior checks. Every allocation, read and write is checked, and it comes out clean.
sanitizers: Then ThreadSanitizer, for concurrency. Readers, writers and the background compaction thread share data safely, without a single race.
crash: The crash campaign kills the writer with SIGKILL at random moments, even in the middle of compaction. It then checks every acknowledged write, and none are lost.
powercut: But a killed process is not a power cut. This shim keeps only what was really fsynced, rebuilds the directory from that, and still nothing is lost.
mutation: Does that test have teeth? Put back the real bug it found, one missing directory fsync, and the very first power cut catches the lost write.
benchmark: Then performance. Twenty thousand fsynced writes, then twenty thousand random reads at well over a million per second, thanks to Bloom filters and a block cache.
ondisk: This is what the engine leaves on disk. There is a write-ahead log per memtable, an append-only MANIFEST, and sorted, checksummed tables.
service: The engine also runs as a Spring Boot service, calling C++ through Java's foreign function API. Its integration tests pass against the real library.
recovery: Finally, recovery over HTTP. We write three keys and kill the server with SIGKILL. After a restart, every acknowledged key is still there.
outro: Leveled compaction, snapshots, a write-ahead log and a MANIFEST, proven under crashes and power cuts. The code and every test are on GitHub.
